The paper targets the radar frequency range of 2.0-18.0 GHz, which covers most modern radar systems.
Type-IV absorber achieves a bandwidth of 14.63 GHz with total thickness of only 3.0 mm.
Type-VII absorber covers the entire 2.0-18.0 GHz range with total thickness of 5.37 mm.
The matching layer uses composite material S₁ (10% CIP) with lower electromagnetic parameters for impedance matching.
The absorbing layer uses composite material S₂ (35% CIP) with higher electromagnetic parameters for energy dissipation.
Particle swarm optimization (PSO) was used to determine optimal layer thicknesses and material configurations.
Seven different multilayered absorber designs were developed and compared through optimization.
Type-IV design shows minimum reflection loss of -17.75 dB at 3.26 GHz.
Type-VII design shows minimum reflection loss of -14.42 dB at 5.14 GHz.
Both Type-IV and Type-VII designs maintain reflection coefficients below -7.0 dB across incident angles from 0° to 45°.
Air gaps were incorporated into Type-V, Type-VI, and Type-VII designs to improve performance.
The cost function for optimization includes four weighted terms: minimum reflection coefficient, total thickness, bandwidth, and average reflection coefficient.
The PEC cylinder used for validation had height and radius of 60 mm each, equivalent to two wavelengths at 10 GHz.
Type-IV coating provided maximum RCS reduction of 17.5 dB at 17 GHz on the PEC cylinder.
Type-VII coating provided maximum RCS reduction of 16.5 dB at 12.0 GHz on the PEC cylinder.
Type-VII coating showed superior performance at lower frequencies compared to Type-IV coating.
Both coatings achieved at least 8.0 dB RCS reduction across most of the 2.0-18.0 GHz frequency band.
The complex permittivity and permeability of S₁ remain relatively constant across the 2.0-18.0 GHz range.
The complex permittivity of S₂ is stable while its complex permeability decreases slightly with frequency.
Single-layer absorbers (Type I and II) demonstrated narrow bandwidth and poor overall performance.
Increasing the number of layers from 1 to 5 progressively improved bandwidth and reflection peak performance.
The transmission line theory approach significantly reduced computational requirements compared to full-wave simulation.
The absorber designs demonstrated insensitivity to both incident angle and polarization of electromagnetic waves.
The paper demonstrates that multilayered designs can achieve ultra-thin profiles while maintaining broad bandwidth.
The research validates that designed absorbers perform effectively on curved surfaces like cylinders, not just infinite planes.
